steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on federated domain adaptation, where we study server aggregation rules (FedDA, FedGP and auto-weighted versions) through a theoretical framework. Motivate the problem, explain the gap in prior work, describe the methods and list the contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Federated learning and the FDA problem
- FL: distributed ML, server aggregates client models, data stays private
- relevant where data heterogeneous / insufficient, e.g. healthcare
- small local hospital can't train generalizable model alone; domain divergence from other hospitals complicates FL
- Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA): source clients + server improve target client
- two hurdles: (i) domain shift source vs target, (ii) data scarcity in target

Prior work and the gap
- recent work on domain shift and limited data in FL
- minimize impact of distribution shift between clients, e.g. personalized FL
- but assume ample data per client; not true for small hospitals in cross-silo FL
- data scarcity = bottleneck; small hospitals lack labeled or unlabeled data
- Unsupervised FDA (UFDA) only when target has abundant unlabeled data (less common)
- gap: both domain shift and data scarcity together under-explored

Focus on aggregation rules; guiding question
- address both FDA challenges by designing server aggregation rules (how server combines source + target updates in each global loop)
- easy to implement: only server changes (e.g. variations of federated averaging) -> main target of innovation in FL
- question: How does one define a “good” FDA aggregation rule?

Theoretical framework, FedDA and FedGP
- no theoretical foundations so far for federated aggregation rules in FDA
- framework with two metrics: (i) source-target divergence, (ii) target data scarcity; used to analyze aggregation rules
- FedDA: simple heuristic, convex combination of source and target gradients; noisy target gradients from limited data still useful signal
- FedGP: filtering-based gradient projection; keeps beneficial parts of source gradients using target gradient (Figure 1); convex combination of target gradient and its positive projection along source gradients
- generalization analysis on target: why FedGP may beat FedDA; projection before convex combination is crucial

Auto-weighting and results
- theory gives optimal weights for combining source and target gradients -> auto-weighted FedGP and FedDA
- under-performing FedDA much better with auto-weighting, competitive with FedGP
- FedGP + auto-weighted versions beat personalized FL and UFDA baselines across datasets
- code: https://github.com/jackyzyb/AutoFedGP

Summary of contributions
- theoretical framework for FDA aggregation rules; answers what a “good” rule is
- FedGP for large domain shift + limited target data
- optimal weight for FedDA and FedGP -> auto-weighting, better performance
- experiments: theory predictive of practice; beat personalized FL and UFDA on ColoredMNIST, VLCS, TerraIncognita, DomainNet

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm where the server aggregates the models of the clients while data privacy is maintained. FL is especially interesting for real-world applications where data heterogeneity and insufficiency are common problems, for example in healthcare. For instance, a small local hospital may have trouble training a generalizable model on its own because it does not have enough data, and the domain divergence from other hospitals makes it even harder to apply FL. A promising framework for this problem is Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA), where source clients work with the server to improve the model performance of a target client. FDA is hard mainly for two reasons: (i) the domain shift between the source and target domains, and (ii) the scarcity of data in the target domain.

Recent works have looked at these challenges of domain shift and limited data in federated settings. Some of them try to minimize the impact of distribution shifts between clients, for example through personalized federated learning. But these works usually assume that all clients have plenty of data, and this assumption may not be true for small hospitals in a cross-silo FL setting. Data scarcity can be a crucial bottleneck in real-world scenarios, for example small hospitals lack data, whether it is labeled or unlabeled. In the special (and arguably less common) case where the target client has a lot of unlabeled data, Unsupervised Federated Domain Adaptation (UFDA) may be useful. Even with this existing work, there is still an under-explored gap in the literature about the case where both challenges, domain shift and data scarcity, are present together.

- address both FDA challenges by designing server aggregation rules (how server combines source + target updates in each global loop)
- easy to implement: only server changes (e.g. variations of federated averaging) -> main target of innovation in FL
- question: How does one define a “good” FDA aggregation rule?

- FedGP: filtering-based gradient projection; keeps beneficial parts of source gradients using target gradient (Figure 1); convex combination of target gradient and its positive projection along source gradients
- generalization analysis on target: why FedGP may beat FedDA; projection before convex combination is crucial

- theory gives optimal weights for combining source and target gradients -> auto-weighted FedGP and FedDA
- under-performing FedDA much better with auto-weighting, competitive with FedGP

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm where the server aggregates the models of the clients while data privacy is maintained. FL is especially interesting for real-world applications where data heterogeneity and insufficiency are common problems, for example in healthcare. For instance, a small local hospital may have trouble training a generalizable model on its own because it does not have enough data, and the domain divergence from other hospitals makes it even harder to apply FL. A promising framework for this problem is Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA), where source clients work with the server to improve the model performance of a target client. FDA is hard mainly for two reasons: (i) the domain shift between the source and target domains, and (ii) the scarcity of data in the target domain.

Recent works have looked at these challenges of domain shift and limited data in federated settings. Some of them try to minimize the impact of distribution shifts between clients, for example through personalized federated learning. But these works usually assume that all clients have plenty of data, and this assumption may not be true for small hospitals in a cross-silo FL setting. Data scarcity can be a crucial bottleneck in real-world scenarios, for example small hospitals lack data, whether it is labeled or unlabeled. In the special (and arguably less common) case where the target client has a lot of unlabeled data, Unsupervised Federated Domain Adaptation (UFDA) may be useful. Even with this existing work, there is still an under-explored gap in the literature about the case where both challenges, domain shift and data scarcity, are present together.

To fill this gap, this work deals directly with the two main challenges of FDA, and it focuses on carefully designing server aggregation rules, that is, the mechanisms the server uses to combine updates across source and target clients in each global optimization loop. We focus on aggregation rules because they are easy to implement, since only the server has to change its operations (e.g., variations of federated averaging), and so they have become the main target of innovation in the federated learning literature. In short, our work is motivated by the question:

How does one define a “good” FDA aggregation rule?

As far as we understand, there are no theoretical foundations that systematically look at how different federated aggregation rules behave in the context of FDA. So we introduce a theoretical framework that defines two metrics to characterize FDA settings, and we use them to analyze the performance of FDA aggregation rules. The metrics characterize (i) the divergence between the source and target domains and (ii) how scarce the training data is in the target domain. Using this framework, we propose and analyze two aggregation approaches. The first one is a simple heuristic, FedDA, which is just a convex combination of source and target gradients. Maybe surprisingly, we find that even noisy gradients, computed from the limited data of the target client, can still give a valuable signal. The second one is a new filtering-based gradient projection method, FedGP. This method is designed to extract and aggregate the beneficial components of the source gradients with the help of the target gradient, as shown in Figure 1. FedGP computes a convex combination of the target gradient and its positive projection along the direction of the source gradients. Interestingly, with a generalization analysis on the target domain, our framework explains why FedGP may outperform FedDA: we find that it is crucial to do the projection operation before the convex combination.

Importantly, our theoretical framework also suggests the optimal weights for combining source and target gradients, and this gives auto-weighted versions of both FedGP and FedDA. In particular, FedDA, which under-performs, gets much better with auto-weighting, enough to be competitive with FedGP, which shows the value of our theory. On many datasets we show that FedGP, as well as auto-weighted FedDA and FedGP, outperform personalized FL and UFDA baselines. Our code is at https://github.com/jackyzyb/AutoFedGP.

Summary of Contributions. Our contributions are theoretical and practical, and they address the FDA problem through federated aggregation in a principled way.

- We introduce a theoretical framework for understanding and analyzing how FDA aggregation rules perform, motivated by the two challenges in FDA. Our theory gives a principled answer to the question: How do we define a “good” FDA aggregation rule?

- We propose FedGP as an effective solution to the FDA challenges of large domain shifts and limited target data.

- Our theory finds the optimal weight parameter for the aggregation rules FedDA and FedGP. This auto-weighting scheme improves performance further.

- Extensive experiments show that our theory predicts what happens in practice. The proposed methods outperform personalized FL and UFDA baselines on the real-world ColoredMNIST, VLCS, TerraIncognita, and DomainNet datasets.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that aggregates clients’ models on the server while maintaining data privacy [1]. FL is especially interesting in real-world applications where data heterogeneity and insufficiency are common issues, such as healthcare settings. For instance, a small local hospital may struggle to train a generalizable model independently due to insufficient data, and the domain divergence from other hospitals further complicates the application of FL. A promising framework for addressing this problem is Federated Domain Adaptation (FDA), where source clients collaborate with the server to enhance the model performance of a target client [2]. FDA is challenging due to two primary factors: (i) the domain shift existing between source and target domains, and (ii) the scarcity of data in the target domain.

Recent works have looked at these challenges of domain shift and limited data in federated settings. Some of these works aim to minimize the impacts of distribution shifts between clients [3,4,5], e.g., via personalized federated learning [6,7,8,9]. However, these studies commonly presume that all clients possess ample data, an assumption that may not hold for small hospitals in a cross-silo FL setting. Data scarcity challenges can be a crucial bottleneck in real-world scenarios, e.g., small hospitals lack data – whether labeled or unlabeled. In the special (and arguably less common) case where the target client has access to abundant unlabeled data, Unsupervised Federated Domain Adaptation (UFDA) [2,10,11] may be useful. Despite this existing work, there is still an under-explored gap in the literature addressing both challenges, namely domain shift and data scarcity, coexist.

To fill the gap, this work directly approaches the two principal challenges associated with FDA, focusing on carefully designing server aggregation rules, i.e., mechanisms used by the server to combine updates across source and target clients within each global optimization loop. We focus on aggregation rules as they are easy to implement – requiring only the server to change its operations (e.g., variations of federated averaging [1]), and thus have become the primary target of innovation in the federated learning literature. In brief, our work is motivated by the question:

How does one define a “good” FDA aggregation rule?

To our understanding, there are no theoretical foundations that systematically examine the behaviors of various federated aggregation rules within the context of the FDA. Therefore, we introduce a theoretical framework that establishes two metrics to characterize the FDA settings and employ them to analyze the performance of FDA aggregation rules. The proposed metrics characterize (i) the divergence between source and target domains and (ii) the level of training data scarcity in the target domain. Leveraging the proposed theoretical framework, we propose and analyze two aggregation approaches. The first is a simple heuristic FedDA, a simple convex combination of source and target gradients. Perhaps surprisingly, we find that even noisy gradients, computed using the limited data of the target client, can still deliver a valuable signal. The second is a novel filtering-based gradient projection method, FedGP. This method is designed to extract and aggregate beneficial components of the source gradients with the assistance of the target gradient, as depicted in Figure 1. FedGP calculates a convex combination of the target gradient and its positive projection along the direction of source gradients. Using a generalization analysis on the target domain, our theoretical framework explains why FedGP may outperform FedDA – specifically, we find that performing the projection operation before the convex combination is crucial.

Importantly, our theoretical framework suggests the optimal weights for combining source and target gradients, leading to auto-weighted versions of both FedGP and FedDA. In particular, we find that the under-performing FedDA is significantly improved by using auto-weighting – enough to be competitive with FedGP, demonstrating the value of our theory. Across extensive datasets, we demonstrate that FedGP, as well as the auto-weighted FedDA and FedGP, outperforms personalized FL and UFDA baselines. Our code is at https://github.com/jackyzyb/AutoFedGP.

Summary of Contributions. Our contributions are both theoretical and practical, addressing the FDA problem through federated aggregation in a principled way.

- • We introduce a theoretical framework understanding and analyzing the performance of FDA aggregation rules, inspired by two challenges existing in FDA. Our theories provide a principled response to the question: How do we define a “good” FDA aggregation rule?

- • We propose FedGP as an effective solution to the FDA challenges of substantial domain shifts and limited target data.

- • Our theory determines the optimal weight parameter for aggregation rules, FedDA and FedGP. This auto-weighting scheme leads to further performance improvements.

- • Extensive experiments show that our theory is predictive of practice. The proposed methods outperform personalized FL and UFDA baselines on real-world ColoredMNIST, VLCS, TerraIncognita, and DomainNet datasets.
